draft.title: Induction
card: Induction is the process of introducing a new employee to the business. It happens when they start, after they have been selected.
The new employee learns about their job, meets the people they will work with, and is shown the workplace safety rules.
They also learn the business's culture, which is its shared values and the usual way people behave and work together.
A good induction helps the employee settle in faster, so they can work well sooner and are more likely to feel part of the team.
draft.remember: Induction helps a new employee settle in by covering the job, people, safety and culture.

a.q: Which of these is part of an induction?
opts: Showing a new employee the safety rules
Advertising the job on a website
Asking applicants to do a sample task
Writing a list of the duties for the role
a.why: Induction happens after someone is hired, and it includes workplace safety. The other options are about finding or choosing staff, or about designing the job, which come before induction.
a.clue: Induction happens after the person has been hired.

b.q: Tom starts at a Geelong cycle shop. On day one his manager introduces him to the team and explains how the shop expects staff to treat customers. What is the main benefit to the shop?
opts: Tom is likely to settle in and work well sooner
Tom no longer needs to learn his duties
Tom has proved he has the skills for the job
Tom is guaranteed to stay with the shop
b.why: Meeting the team and learning how things are done helps a new employee settle in faster. It does not prove skills, as he is already hired, and it cannot guarantee he will stay.
b.clue: Think about how quickly a new person feels at home.

a.best: Showing a new employee the safety rules

b.best: Tom is likely to settle in and work well sooner

problems.detail: The clue ('Think about how quickly a new person feels at home') points straight at the 'settle in ... sooner' option, so a student can answer without knowing the idea.
The right option is the only hedged one ('likely'). The distractors use absolutes ('proved', 'no longer', 'guaranteed'), so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
